rows.text: If I have not written to His Holiness and to Your Most Illustrious Lordship as often as duty commands, two things have prevented me. The
first is that it is difficult to tell the truth without someone among them finding his interests affected. The other is that affairs are handled by
so many hands, with such different passions, that we are in such uncertainty that our destruction seems inevitable. The prospect
of our loss could not fail to cause His Holiness extreme displeasure, and I shall avoid, as far as I can,
being the bearer of bad news. Thus I had resolved to write no more to him or to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, had your letter
of 1 June not assured me that His Holiness had welcomed the very particular account I ventured to give him
of events here, and my freely telling him what I thought of them. Although many new things have happened since my
letters, Your Lordship will find that in fact I was not mistaken, and that people would not remedy matters in time, either when I was
over there or since. In the end, unless God intervenes, I see the cause of the Catholic religion in this kingdom in a bad way,
for several reasons I could tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship, beyond what I explain to His Holiness on the subject. Moreover,
everything he is told by those who have exercised that ministry here for the Holy See seems to be treated as so many oracles, leaving no credit for the
truth—which will now be found to be as I have always stated it, at the risk of my head. From Monsieur Mateouci
down to the present state of things, they alone have brought more ruin to affairs than the enemies have, so full have
they been of I know not what that does not suit us, or of little experience of our dispositions, and of passion.
And if I have put anything forward in the account I am giving His Holiness about the conduct of the said Mateuci,
the slightest letter anyone might write to me will always bring me to appear wherever they wish, to maintain it to his face. As for Monsieur de
Malvoisie, I was not there when he and Mayenne fell into discord. Nevertheless,
the legate’s nephew has complained to me of it; besides, it is difficult to contradict a general report. Your Lordship
can also consider for yourself that the King of Spain’s army has done nothing but remain on the frontier,
bringing disgrace upon so great a monarch, and has withdrawn merely at a rumour that Navarre
was coming to seek it out. Furthermore, the legate, without any consideration whatever, wants us to proceed
to the election of a king just when the enemy is beginning to win the voices of many who were his
enemies, through his appearance of wishing to become Catholic, and is to attend
Mass on Sunday. Having nothing with which to resist him except promises by which we have been so often
deceived, we would need many deeds before we could be made to reject the prospect
of peace. It will be no small achievement if we temper it into a truce. Everyone is
tired of being a laughingstock to all Christendom, and of seeing themselves abandoned, only to
end by breathing their last. As for promises, our enemies are not without them: they
offer to show letters from Your Most Illustrious Lordship concerning his reception if he becomes Catholic. The Holy
See is weary of continuing its expenditure, which one may say amounted to something during the pontificate of
Pope Gregory. But since then it would have been better for it had we been denied
all hope of aid outright, so that we might take a definite resolution.
Let Your Most Illustrious Lordship only remember how insistently I asked for a member of
the House of Bourbon, and the refusal I received; then for the Infanta’s marriage to one of our
princes. I was refused outright, the matter being referred to the legate and the Duke of Feria. I think I
made it quite clear that we would never hazard our religion, honours
and lives without firmer assurances, and unless His Holiness spoke more plainly. We want
assurances from him alone, as the party most concerned; otherwise we
should not be in a position to do better in future than in the past. I would have been very imprudent not to act
otherwise, knowing the Spaniards as I do. That made me reject the candidate
proposed to me by His Holiness, who in truth would have been the best; but one needed a clear and
certain prospect. Even if my master had been willing to let himself be drawn into it, no one would have
resisted him more than I. And where would he be now? The enemies
still offer to show a letter from His Holiness to the legate, instructing him
to do nothing to the prejudice of the House of Bourbon, against the fundamental laws
of the kingdom, or against the Catholics who support Navarre—something very contrary to
so many assurances made to me. I have said it, and shall say it until I die: if harm
comes of it, people have willed it so. We have not failed to point out everything possible,
having no passion other than religion. Yet we remain amid these uncertainties while
the others take advantage of the opportunity. Are they not doing well? For all our
pains I still expect a world of reproaches, all falling upon Mayenne, who does more than he
ought without any fear; for honour is worth more than all the appearances
sought by most men, and the end will crown the work. For, at a time when
everyone is banded together to tear apart our State—which would then bring the ruin of
Christendom—abandoned by everyone, all his warnings disregarded, and
mocked over them by people who, apart from being ministers of a great prince, would not be
above the rank or of too good a family to serve as servants, he takes heart
against every kind of tempest. He works to provide the supreme and sole remedy, his presence,
to prevent the imminent fall of the State and religion. There can be no doubt that
some will wish, as is their custom, to cover their malice with a world of
falsehoods. But if their design has been made vain, there is no lack of people able
to write good defences. They will make the shame people would cast
upon faces marked only by honour and magnanimity fall back upon its authors. Would to
God that His Holiness knew as I do how his ministers have behaved, their self-interest, and that of
those who present themselves as nothing but religious, when there is only pure ambition, all too evident
despite countless protestations to the contrary. There would have been no means of
answering for it had the legate not intervened, in a matter in which His Holiness’s honour has been
greatly implicated. I speak of these affairs to Your Most Illustrious Lordship at great length. Indeed, if I did not fear
importuning you, there would be enough to fill eight times as much paper. To avoid being too tedious, I shall say that
if you knew, as I do, the artifice of our friends, what they have and do, their weakness, how
the legate has shown himself their partisan in tearing apart our poor State to the detriment of
the Holy See’s honour, and a world of other things, you would marvel a thousand times over at
Mayenne’s patience. That patience has extended even to being willing to accept Monsieur Guise as king, provided
they showed him how he could be defended. But they want us to believe mere words,
as though there were any prospect of giving further trust to people who have never
shown us any, and whose guiding principle is to deceive us. Perhaps you will even
find it strange that I have drawn your attention to the two points the enemies
are circulating, both about His Holiness’s letter and about yours in particular. But it seems to me right that Your Lordship
should know everything, so that you can provide for it. It is true, as I have declared often enough, that if His Holiness is pleased to communicate his
intentions for Mayenne through me, without interposing the legate, Mayenne will take only His Holiness’s commands as his rule.
Besides, things have reached such a pass between them that, were it not for respect for His Holiness, the legate
would no longer play for so long at Mayenne’s expense, or with the ruin of everyone in his household.
Indeed, he has been so disrespectful that he has made him fear being
in His Holiness’s disfavour. Everyone nevertheless thinks this is a device to achieve
his designs and oblige the Spaniard, which has always been his principal aim.

closing:
Most Illustrious Lord,
I most humbly beseech the Creator to grant Your Most Illustrious Lordship a very happy and very long life. Paris, [22] July 1593.
D. V. S. I.
Your very humble and very obedient servant,
Desportes.
